topic.subject: social
topic.title: Parliament and the making of laws
topic.scope: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, elections, how a bill becomes law, role of the opposition, unpopular laws

misconceptions.statement: The Rajya Sabha is more powerful than the Lok Sabha because it is the 'Upper House'.
misconceptions.why: Students equate the word 'upper' with higher authority or power in a hierarchy.
misconceptions.fix: The Lok Sabha is more powerful because its members are directly elected by the people, and it controls the executive.

probe.question: If the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha disagree on a money bill, who prevails?
probe.wrong_answer: The Rajya Sabha because it is the Upper House.

misconceptions.root_belief: Words have their literal everyday meaning.

misconceptions.statement: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the citizens of India.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the election of local MPs with the direct election of the head of government.
misconceptions.fix: Citizens elect MPs to the Lok Sabha; the party with the majority then selects their leader to be the Prime Minister.

probe.question: Who do you vote for in a general election?
probe.wrong_answer: I vote for the Prime Minister.

misconceptions.root_belief: One event has one single cause.

misconceptions.statement: The President can reject any law passed by Parliament if they do not like it.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the President acts like a monarch or a supreme ruler with absolute veto power.
misconceptions.fix: The President is a constitutional head and must sign a bill once it is passed by both houses of Parliament.

probe.question: Can the President stop a bill from becoming law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if they disagree with the law.

misconceptions.root_belief: Authority figures have absolute personal power.

misconceptions.statement: The role of the opposition is to stop all government work.
misconceptions.why: Students see opposition in media as mere fighting and assume the goal is obstructionism.
misconceptions.fix: The opposition highlights flaws in policies and ensures the government remains accountable to the public.

probe.question: What is the main job of the opposition party?
probe.wrong_answer: To block every law the government proposes.

misconceptions.statement: Laws are only changed when the government decides to change them.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the role of civil society and public pressure in the legislative process.
misconceptions.fix: Citizens can influence the law-making process through protests, media campaigns, and public opinion.

probe.question: How can a law be changed if it is unpopular?
probe.wrong_answer: Only the government can decide to change it.

misconceptions.root_belief: Power flows only from the top down.

misconceptions.statement: All members of the Lok Sabha are chosen by the President.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the nominated members of the Rajya Sabha with the Lok Sabha, and think top officials appoint the 'main' house.
misconceptions.fix: Lok Sabha members are elected directly by adult citizens (18+) from constituencies through general elections, usually every five years.

probe.question: How does a person become a Member of the Lok Sabha?

misconceptions.root_belief: Top officials appoint legislators rather than voters electing them
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom discussion / NCERT Social and Political Life

misconceptions.statement: Citizens vote directly to choose the members of the Rajya Sabha.
misconceptions.why: Students assume every house of Parliament is elected the same way as the Lok Sabha.
misconceptions.fix: Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (and a few are nominated by the President for their work in arts, science, etc.).

probe.question: Who votes to elect Rajya Sabha members?
probe.wrong_answer: All adult citizens vote for them in the general election.

misconceptions.root_belief: All legislative houses are elected the same way

misconceptions.statement: Only the Prime Minister can introduce a bill in Parliament.
misconceptions.why: Students link lawmaking only with the most visible leader of the government.
misconceptions.fix: A bill can be introduced by a minister (government bill) or by any other member of Parliament (private member's bill), in either house (money bills only in the Lok Sabha).

probe.question: Who can bring a new bill before Parliament?

misconceptions.root_belief: Only the top leader can start lawmaking

misconceptions.statement: A bill becomes a law as soon as the Lok Sabha passes it.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the Lok Sabha as the whole Parliament because it is the more prominent house.
misconceptions.fix: An ordinary bill must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (in the same form) and then get the President's assent before it becomes law.

probe.question: A bill has just been passed by the Lok Sabha. Is it now a law?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the Lok Sabha passing it is enough to make it a law.

misconceptions.root_belief: One house alone is the whole Parliament

misconceptions.statement: A bill is voted on immediately after it is introduced, without any discussion.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine lawmaking as a single vote instead of a series of stages.
misconceptions.fix: A bill goes through stages: introduction (first reading), detailed discussion and debate, often examination by a committee, amendments, and then voting.

probe.question: What happens right after a bill is introduced in the House?
probe.wrong_answer: Members vote on it straight away with no debate.

misconceptions.statement: Public protests and media have no role in the making of laws in a democracy.
misconceptions.why: Students think only elected members and the government matter once elections are over.
misconceptions.fix: Citizens can express opinions through peaceful protests, petitions, the media and meetings with representatives; this public pressure can lead Parliament to debate, amend or make laws (e.g., the Right to Information Act).

probe.question: Can a citizens' campaign influence what law Parliament makes?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only MPs decide laws and the public cannot affect them.

misconceptions.statement: A person from the party that gets the most votes in a constituency becomes the MP only if they get more than half of all votes.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the idea of 'majority' as more than 50% to constituency results.
misconceptions.fix: In a constituency the candidate who gets the highest number of votes wins, even if that is less than half of the total votes cast.

probe.question: In a constituency, A gets 40 votes, B gets 35 and C gets 25. Who wins?
probe.wrong_answer: No one wins because nobody has more than 50 votes.

misconceptions.root_belief: Winning always requires more than half the votes
